write.desc: This topic defines an infinite series as the limit of its sequence of partial sums and draws the first consequences of that definition (geometric and telescoping sums, linearity, tails, the term test, the harmonic series and the Cauchy criterion), so that every later statement about series is seen as a theorem about a sequence.

points.name: Series, partial sums and the sum of a series
points.what: The learner can define the partial sums s_n of a series, define convergence of the series as convergence of (s_n) and its sum as the limit, recognise divergence including divergence to plus or minus infinity, and explain why an infinite sum is not computed by 'adding forever' but defined by a limit.
outside: definition of the limit of a sequence (epsilon-N)
sequences diverging to plus or minus infinity

points.name: Geometric series
points.what: The learner can derive the closed form (1 - r^(n+1))/(1 - r) for the partial sums of a geometric series and prove from it that the series converges to 1/(1 - r) exactly when |r| < 1 and diverges otherwise.
outside: limit of r^n: tends to 0 when |r| < 1 and does not converge when |r| > 1 or r = -1

points.name: Telescoping series
points.what: The learner can recognise a series whose terms are differences b_n - b_(n+1), compute its partial sums exactly, and prove convergence and find the sum, as in the sum of 1/(n(n+1)) = 1, using partial fractions where needed.

points.name: Linearity of convergent series
points.what: The learner can prove from the sequence limit laws that the sum of two convergent series and a constant multiple of a convergent series converge to the expected sums, and knows that a convergent plus a divergent series diverges while two divergent series may have a convergent sum, so series cannot be split carelessly.
outside: algebraic limit laws for sums and constant multiples of convergent sequences

points.name: Changing finitely many terms and tails
points.what: The learner can prove that changing, adding or deleting finitely many terms does not affect whether a series converges (only its sum), define the tail sum from index N on, and show that the tails of a convergent series tend to zero.
outside: a sequence and its shifted sequence have the same limit behaviour

points.name: The term test (nth-term test for divergence)
points.what: The learner can prove that if a series converges then its terms tend to zero (from a_n = s_n - s_(n-1)), use the contrapositive to prove divergence, and explain why terms tending to zero can never by itself prove convergence.
outside: algebraic limit laws for differences of convergent sequences

points.name: The harmonic series diverges
points.what: The learner can prove that the sum of 1/n diverges to infinity by grouping terms into blocks to show s_(2^k) >= 1 + k/2, and uses it as the standard example of a series whose terms tend to zero but which diverges.
outside: an increasing sequence that is unbounded above diverges to plus infinity

points.name: Cauchy criterion for series
points.what: The learner can state and derive from the Cauchy criterion for sequences that a series converges if and only if for every epsilon > 0 there is N with |a_(m+1) + ... + a_n| < epsilon for all n > m >= N, and use it to prove convergence without knowing the sum, to recover the term test as the case of one term, and to show the harmonic series diverges because s_(2n) - s_n >= 1/2.
outside: Cauchy criterion for sequences: a real sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.7 Properties of Infinite Series; harmonic series in Section 2.4

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis (4th ed.)
Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
